claim: Speech perception arises from internal models of how specific sensory features are associated with speech sounds.
source: Speech perception presumably arises from internal models of how specific sensory features are associated with speech sounds.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement presented in the abstract without direct experimental support in this manuscript, though it is based on established theoretical frameworks.

claim: Sensory features associated with speech sounds change constantly due to factors like different speakers and articulation modes.
source: These features change constantly (e.g. different speakers, articulation modes etc.)
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about speech variability.

claim: Listeners need to recalibrate their internal models by appropriately weighing new versus old evidence.
source: listeners need to recalibrate their internal models by appropriately weighing new versus old evidence.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim that forms the basis of the study's hypothesis.

claim: Classical models of speech recalibration ignore volatility.
source: Models of speech recalibration classically ignore this volatility.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature throughout the manuscript.

claim: The effect of volatility in tasks where sensory cues were associated with arbitrary experimenter-defined categories were well described by models that continuously adapt the learning rate while keeping a single representation of the category.
source: The effect of volatility in tasks where sensory cues were associated with arbitrary experimenter-defined categories were well described by models that continuously adapt the learning rate while keeping a single representation of the category.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Behrens et al., 2007; Mathys et al., 2011) mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: Recalibration of natural speech sound categories is better described by representing categories at different time scales.
source: Using neurocomputational modelling we show that recalibration of natural speech sound categories is better described by representing the latter at different time scales.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Working representations of speech categories are driven both by their current environment and their long-term memory representations.
source: We propose that working representations of speech categories are driven both by their current environment and their long-term memory representations.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by the modeling results.

claim: Neurocognitive adaptation to varying stimuli can be driven by an explicit external feedback signal.
source: Neurocognitive adaptation to varying stimuli can be driven by an explicit external feedback signal
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Neurocognitive adaptation can take place with simple passive exposure to a changing stimulus environment via implicit statistical learning.
source: but might also take place with simple passive exposure to a changing stimulus environment via implicit statistical learning (Saffran et al., 1996; Gilbert et al., 2001; Barascud et al., 2016; Schwiedrzik et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Neural representations of speech sound categories are susceptible to stimulus-driven recalibration.
source: In the domain of speech perception, neural representations of sound categories are susceptible to stimulus-driven recalibration.
evidence: This is supported by the citations that follow in the manuscript.

claim: The perception of unclear or ambiguous speech stimuli that have previously been disambiguated by context is biased by the disambiguating percept.
source: Typically, the perception of unclear or ambiguous speech stimuli that have previously been disambiguated by context (McQueen et al., 2006; Clarke and Luce, 2005) or by a concurrent visual stimulus (Bertelson et al., 2003; Vroomen et al., 2007) is biased by the disambiguating percept.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Simple exposure to novel statistics results in a modified slope in psychometric functions and changes the way listeners classify stimuli.
source: Even simple exposure to novel statistics e.g., a variation in the spread of sensory features characteristic of stop consonants, quickly results in a modified slope in psychometric functions, and changes the way listeners classify stimuli (Clayards et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Acoustic representations are modified after altered auditory feedback during production.
source: Interestingly, acoustic representations are also modified after altered auditory feedback during production (Nasir and Ostry, 2009; Lametti et al., 2014; Patri et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Speech sound categories remain largely plastic in adulthood.
source: These observations illustrate that speech sound categories remain largely plastic in adulthood.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies on speech recalibration.

claim: Changes in acoustic speech categories can be induced by input from the visual modality.
source: Using two-alternative forced choice tasks, studies have shown that changes in acoustic speech categories can be induced by input from the visual modality (e.g. Bertelson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Acoustic information can disambiguate lipreading, resulting in measurable categorization aftereffects.
source: Reciprocally, acoustic information can also disambiguate lipreading (Baart and Vroomen, 2010), resulting in measurable categorization aftereffects.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Recalibration can occur very rapidly, with effects being observable after a single exposure.
source: While such effects can be observed after repeated exposure to the adapting stimuli, recalibration can also occur very rapidly, with effects being observable after a single exposure (Vroomen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Fast and dynamic recalibration has been modelled as incremental Bayesian updating where internal perceptual categories track the stimulus statistics.
source: This fast and dynamic process has been modelled as incremental Bayesian updating (Kleinschmidt and Jaeger, 2015) where internal perceptual categories track the stimulus statistics.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous modeling work.

claim: The incremental Bayesian updating model weighs all evidence equally, disregarding their recency.
source: The resulting recalibration weighs all evidence equally, disregarding their recency.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of the cited model.

claim: The incremental Bayesian updating model successfully describes perceptual changes observed when listeners are confronted with repeated presentations of a single modified version of a speech sound.
source: The model hence successfully describes perceptual changes observed when listeners are confronted with repeated presentations of a single modified version of a speech sound.
evidence: This is an inference about the capabilities of the cited model.

claim: The incremental Bayesian updating model cannot appropriately deal with intrinsically changing environments, in which sensory cues quickly become obsolete.
source: However, it cannot appropriately deal with intrinsically changing environments, in which sensory cues quickly become obsolete.
evidence: This is a theoretical critique of the cited model.

claim: Real moment to moment physical changes in the environment are referred to as 'volatility' to distinguish them from the trial-by-trial response variability observed in a fixed environment.
source: Real moment to moment physical changes in the environment are referred to as 'volatility' to distinguish them from the trial-by-trial response variability observed in a fixed environment.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors.

claim: Humans are able to adjust their learning rate to the volatility in the stimulus set, with faster learning rates in more volatile environments.
source: These studies suggest that humans are able to adjust their learning rate to the volatility in the stimulus set, with faster learning rates (implying a stronger devaluation of recent past evidence) in more volatile environments.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on decision making.

claim: Previous normative models focus on the online estimation of volatility, in which task-relevant features are represented at a single variable time scale.
source: This has led to normative models focussing on the online estimation of volatility, in which task-relevant features are represented at a single variable time scale (Behrens et al., 2007; Mathys et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling work.

claim: The notion of variable learning rates likely also applies to speech processing.
source: The notion of variable learning rates likely also applies to speech processing.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: When recalibrating natural speech categories, a normative model should take into account that these categories may themselves change at different time scales.
source: However, we propose that when recalibrating natural speech categories, a normative model should additionally take into account that these categories may themselves change at different time scales.
evidence: This is the main theoretical proposal of the study.

claim: Transient acoustic changes within a given speech sound category, such as those coming from a new speaker, must not interfere with the long-term representation of that category that should be invariant to speakers.
source: For example, transient acoustic changes within a given speech sound category, such as those coming from a new speaker, must not interfere with the long-term representation of that category that should be invariant for example to speakers.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument supporting the main hypothesis.

claim: Speech sound categories could be represented by more than a single varying timescale.
source: We therefore hypothesize that speech sound categories could be represented by more than a single varying timescale.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study.

claim: Lüttke and collaborators found evidence for recalibration in an experiment that included audio-visual McGurk stimuli shown without an explicit adapting condition.
source: Although speech category recalibration has not been systematically studied in variable environments, Lüttke and collaborators (Lüttke et al., 2016a; Lüttke et al., 2018) found evidence for recalibration in an experiment that included audio-visual McGurk stimuli shown without an explicit adapting condition.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: The first Lüttke study involved six different vowel/consonant/vowel stimuli presented in random order, and recalibration was observed even when acoustic stimuli were not ambiguous.
source: The first study involved six different vowel/consonant/vowel stimuli presented in random order, and recalibration was observed even when acoustic stimuli were not ambiguous (e.g. the /aba/ sound in the McGurk trials).
evidence: This is a description of previous experimental findings.

claim: An acoustic stimulus /aba/ is mostly perceived as an illusory /ada/ when presented with the video of a speaker producing /aga/ (the McGurk effect).
source: The McGurk effect (the fact that an acoustic stimulus /aba/is mostly perceived as an illusory/ada/ when presented with the video of a speaker producing /aga/)
evidence: This is a description of the well-known McGurk effect.

claim: The McGurk effect was powerful enough to yield observable adaptive effects across consecutive trials.
source: was powerful enough to yield observable adaptive effects across consecutive trials.
evidence: This is based on the cited experimental findings.

claim: The probability of an acoustic /aba/ to be categorized as /ada/ was higher when the trial was preceded by an audio-visual McGurk fusion.
source: Specifically, the probability of an acoustic/aba/ to be categorized as/ada/, was higher when the trial was preceded by an audio-visual McGurk fusion.
evidence: This is a description of previous experimental findings.

claim: Recalibration effects do not generalize to all phonetic contrasts/categories.
source: Recalibration effects do not generalize to all phonetic contrasts/categories (Reinisch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: After participants had recalibrated acoustic sounds in the /aba/-/ada/ continuum, recalibration was neither present for /ibi/-/idi/ nor for /ama/-/ana/ or /ubu/-/udu/ continua.
source: After participants had recalibrated acoustic sounds in the /aba /- /ada/continuum (on the basis of acoustic formant transitions), recalibration was neither present for /ibi /- /idi/ (cued by burst and frication), nor for /ama/- /ana/or to /ubu/- /udu/continua (both cued by formant transitions).
evidence: This is a description of previous experimental findings.

claim: In a word recognition task, participants were able to keep different F0/VOT correlation statistics for different places of articulation.
source: Likewise, in a word recognition task, participants were able to keep different F0/VOT (fundamental frequency/voice onset time) correlation statistics for different places of articulation (Idemaru and Holt, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Very short-term changes can modify the internal mapping between sensory features and sublexical speech categories rather than phonemic categories.
source: Based on this failure to generalize, we hypothesized that very short-term changes can modify the internal mapping between sensory features and sublexical speech categories rather than phonemic categories.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from previous experimental findings.

claim: The model divides the process in two steps: perceptual inference and internal model recalibration.
source: The model divides the process in two steps: perceptual inference and internal model recalibration.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: During perceptual inference the model takes the sensory input and infers a perceived speech category, by choosing the category that minimizes sensory prediction error.
source: During perceptual inference the model takes the sensory input and infers a perceived speech category, by choosing the category that minimizes sensory prediction error.
evidence: This is a description of the model's perceptual inference process.

claim: Residual prediction errors might remain following perceptual inference, typically after McGurk fusion.
source: However, 'residual' prediction errors might remain following perceptual inference. This is typically the case after McGurk fusion; since the best explanation for the multisensory input, 'ada', is neither the audio /aba/ nor the visual /aga/, 'residual' prediction errors remain in both acoustic and visual modalities.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the model's behavior.

claim: The best match to the experimental results was obtained when adaptation included two different time scales.
source: The best match to the experimental results described above (Lüttke et al., 2016a) was obtained when we considered that adaptation included two different time scales
evidence: This is the main finding of the modeling study.

claim: Adaptation results in a transient effect leading to recalibration towards the most recently presented stimulus features, decaying towards a longer-lasting representation.
source: resulting in 1) a transient effect leading to recalibration towards the most recently presented stimulus features, decaying towards 2) a longer-lasting representation corresponding to a mapping between category and stimulus features determined within a longer time span.
evidence: This is a description of the model's behavior based on simulation results.

claim: These findings are consistent with theories that posit that the brain continuously recalibrates generative (forward) models to maintain self-consistency.
source: Overall, these findings are consistent with theories that posit that the brain continuously recalibrates generative (forward) models to maintain self-consistency (e.g., Friston et al., 2010)
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citation.

claim: The model offers a neuro-computationally plausible implementation to resolve cognitive conflicts, which can sometimes appear as irrational behaviors.
source: and offers a neuro-computationally plausible implementation to resolve cognitive conflicts, which can sometimes appear as irrational behaviors, such as in post-choice re-evaluation of alternatives (Coppin et al., 2010; Izuma et al., 2010; Colosio et al., 2017; Otten et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations to related work.

claim: Lüttke et al. selected participants with high percentage of fused percepts for McGurk stimuli.
source: In a re-assessment of an existing dataset (Lüttke et al., 2016a) selected participants with high percentage of fused percepts for McGurk stimuli.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology from the cited study.

claim: When presented with acoustic /aba/ together with a video of a speaker articulating /aga/ the most frequent percept was /ada/.
source: When presented with acoustic /aba/ together with a video of a speaker articulating /aga/ the most frequent percept was /ada/
evidence: This is a description of experimental results from the cited study.

claim: Listeners were combining information from acoustic and visual modalities since the same /aba/ acoustic token was correctly categorized as /aba/ when presented alone.
source: These listeners were combining information from acoustic (A) and visual (V) modalities since the same /aba/ acoustic token was correctly categorized as /aba/ when presented alone.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: After a fused McGurk trial, participants showed recalibration, classifying acoustic only /aba/ stimuli as 'ada' more frequently (29%) than when the acoustic only /aba/ was presented after any other stimulus (16%).
source: After a fused McGurk trial, participants showed recalibration. They classified acoustic only /aba/ stimuli as 'ada' more frequently (29% 'ada' percepts) than when the acoustic only /aba/was presented after any other stimulus (16% 'ada' percepts).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results from the cited study.

claim: The assessment involved three acoustic only stimuli with sounds corresponding to /aba/, /ada/ or /aga/; and three audiovisual stimuli – congruent /aba/, congruent /ada/, and the McGurk stimulus.
source: The assessment involved three acoustic only stimuli with sounds corresponding to /aba/, /ada/ or/aga/; and three audiovisual stimuli – congruent /aba/, congruent /ada/, and the McGurk stimulus (acoustic /aba/with video of /aga/).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The model characterized sensory input with a visual feature (the amplitude of lip closure during the transition between the two vowels) and an acoustic feature (the amplitude of the 2nd formant transition).
source: We characterized sensory input with a visual feature, the amplitude of lip closure during the transition between the two vowels (sV); and an acoustic feature, the amplitude of the 2nd formant transition (sA).
evidence: This is a description of the model's feature representation.

claim: The model qualitatively reproduces the average performance across participants in the task.
source: The model qualitatively reproduces the average performance across participants in the task.
evidence: This is a claim about the model's performance supported by simulation results.

claim: The model was chosen with parameters that elicit a very high rate of McGurk percepts.
source: We chose parameters that elicit a very high rate of McGurk percepts (Figure 2, middle panel of the bottom row)
evidence: This is a description of the model parameterization, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The model assumes that listeners were always integrating the two sensory streams.
source: and assumed that listeners were always integrating the two sensory streams.
evidence: This is an assumption made in the model.

claim: After each trial, the model changed the generative model's location parameters associated with the perceived category.
source: After each trial, we changed the generative model's location parameters associated with the perceived category (θk,V θk,A), which represent the categories through their expected sensory feature values in each modality.
evidence: This is a description of the model's recalibration mechanism.

claim: Changes in model parameters were driven by residual sensory prediction error, the difference between the expected and observed values for the modulation amplitudes in each modality.
source: The changes are thus driven by residual sensory prediction error, the difference between the expected and observed values for the modulation amplitudes in each modality.
evidence: This is a description of the model's learning mechanism.

claim: When listeners consistently reported the fused percept 'ada' when confronted with a video of /aga/ and the sound of /aba/, the presence of the visual stream modified the acoustic percept from 'aba' to 'ada'.
source: When listeners consistently reported the fused percept 'ada' when confronted with a video of /aga/ and the sound of /aba/, the presence of the visual stream modified the acoustic percept from 'aba' to 'ada'.
evidence: This is a description of the McGurk effect in the context of the model.

claim: Since the acoustic input did not correspond to the one that was most expected from the perceived token, there was a systematic residual sensory prediction error.
source: Given that the acoustic input did not correspond to the one that was most expected from the perceived token, there was a systematic residual sensory prediction error.
evidence: This is an inference about the model's internal state during McGurk trials.

claim: Since residual prediction error was used as a signal to drive the model's adaptation, the /ada/ representation moved towards the McGurk stimulus parameters after a fused percept.
source: Since this residual prediction error was used as a signal to drive the model's adaptation, the /ada/ representation moved towards the McGurk stimulus parameters after a fused percept (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a description of the model's behavior with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: For the simulation with the closest fit to the McGurk contrast in the no recalibration model, the percentage of acoustic /aba/ categorized as 'ada' was 14% after fused McGurk stimuli and 15% after the control stimuli.
source: For the simulation with the closest fit to the McGurk contrast, the percentage of acoustic /aba/ categorized as 'ada' was 14% after fused McGurk stimuli and 15% after the control stimuli (Wilcoxon signed-rank test p=0.6, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a report of simulation results with statistical testing.

claim: For the no recalibration model, the 95% CI for the difference between trials preceded or not by a fused McGurk stimulus was [-6.48, 5.25]%.
source: The 95% CI for the difference between trials preceded or not by a fused McGurk stimulus was [−6.48, 5.25]%.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the simulations.

claim: For the Bayesian updating model with the closest fit to the McGurk contrast, the percentage of /ada/ responses to acoustic only /aba/ stimuli was 23% after fused McGurk stimuli and 22% after control stimuli, a difference that was not significant.
source: The percentage of /ada/ responses to acoustic only /aba/ stimuli was 23% after fused McGurk stimuli and 22% after control stimuli. This difference was not significant (Wilcoxon signed-rank test p=0.7, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a report of simulation results with statistical testing.

claim: The Bayesian update rule failed to reproduce the McGurk contrast effect of interest.
source: The 95% confidence interval for the difference in medians between the two conditions was [−6.14, 7.97]%, thus failing to reproduce the effect of interest.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Bayesian update rules have the form of a delta rule with a decreasing learning rate.
source: This might be due to the fact that Bayesian update rules have the form of a delta rule with a decreasing learning rate.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the properties of Bayesian update rules.

claim: As a consequence of the decreasing learning rate, the magnitude of changes in the categories diminishes as the experiment progresses and all stimuli end up being related to the same internal model.
source: As a consequence, the magnitude of changes in the categories diminishes as the experiment progresses and all stimuli end up being related to the same internal model.
evidence: This is an inference about the behavior of the Bayesian model.

claim: The Bayesian updates led to an overall increase of /ada/ responses to acoustic /aba/ (24% vs. the 14% of the control experiment without parameter updates).
source: The updates did lead to observable effects; there was an overall increase of /ada/ responses to acoustic /aba/(24% vs. the 14% of the control experiment without parameter updates).
evidence: This is a comparison of simulation results between models.

claim: For the constant delta rule model, the percentage of acoustic /aba/ categorized as 'ada' was not significantly higher when the preceding trial was a fused McGurk trial compared with any other stimulus (27% vs. 24%).
source: As Figure 4C shows, the percentage of acoustic /aba/ categorized as 'ada' was not significantly higher when the preceding trial was a fused McGurk trial compared with any other stimulus (27% vs. 24%, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.08 Figure 4C; median difference at 95% CI [−0.14 12]%).
evidence: This is a report of simulation results with statistical testing.

claim: For the constant delta rule, the proportion of /ada/ responses for acoustic /aba/ inputs is increased compared with simulations run without any adaptation.
source: Note that in this case too, the proportion of /ada/ responses for acoustic /aba/ inputs is increased compared with simulations run without any adaptation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a comparison of simulation results between models.

claim: For the hierarchical updates with intrinsic decay model, the percentage of acoustic /aba/ categorized as 'ada' after control trials was 18% vs. 29% after fused McGurk, a significant difference.
source: The percentage of acoustic /aba/categorized as 'ada' after control trials was 18% vs. 29% after fused McGurk (Wilcoxon ranked-signed test, p=0.0004), the median difference being 95% CI: [5.8, 18.0]%.
evidence: This is a report of simulation results with statistical testing.

claim: The hierarchical update with decay model showed both the overall increase in acoustic /aba/ categorized as /ada/ and the rapid recalibration effect reflected in the specific increase observed when acoustic /aba/ was preceded by a fused McGurk trial.
source: Therefore two effects can be observed; the overall increase in acoustic /aba/ categorized as /ada/ and the rapid recalibration effect reflected in the specific increase observed when acoustic /aba/ was preceded by a fused McGurk trial.
evidence: This is a summary of the simulation results for the hierarchical model.

claim: The ideal adapter Bayesian account was incompatible with the experimental findings, due to the erroneous underlying assumption of a stable environment.
source: With this approach, the ideal adapter Bayesian account turned out to be incompatible with the experimental findings, due to the erroneous underlying assumption of a stable environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Because the Bayesian model assumes that all the sensory observations are derived from exactly the same non-changing distributions, past observations do not lose validity with time.
source: Because the model assumes that all the sensory observations are derived from exactly the same non-changing distributions, past observations do not lose validity with time.
evidence: This is an explanation of the Bayesian model's assumptions.

claim: As the occurrence of a perceived category increases in the Bayesian model, the size of recalibration decreases, until categorization differences across successive trials are no longer observable.
source: As the occurrence of a perceived category increases, the size of recalibration decreases, until categorization differences across successive trials are no longer observable (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a description of the Bayesian model's behavior with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: The 'delta rule' and the 'hierarchical update with decay' both involve a constant learning rate implying that the parameter changes following each perceptual decision do not decrease as the experiment progresses.
source: The 'delta rule' and the 'hierarchical update with decay' both involve a constant learning rate implying that the parameter changes following each perceptual decision do not decrease as the experiment progresses (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is a comparison of model properties with reference to Figure 5B-C.

claim: Although both the delta rule and hierarchical update with decay models were able to qualitatively reproduce the main result, the delta rule without decay did not provide a good fit.
source: Although both models were able to qualitatively reproduce the main result, namely that the rate of acoustic /aba/ categorized as 'ada' was higher immediately after a fused McGurk trial, the delta rule without decay did not provide a good fit.
evidence: This is a comparison of model performance.

claim: The 'hierarchical update with decay' provided the best explanation for the experimental results.
source: The 'hierarchical update with decay' provided the best explanation for the experimental results.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the model comparison.

claim: The advantage of the 'hierarchical update with decay' over the 'delta rule' is that the update decays across trials after a perceptual decision towards a less volatile representation of the category, providing an effective empirical prior.
source: Specifically, its advantage over the 'delta rule' is that the update decays across trials after a perceptual decision towards a less volatile representation of the category, providing an effective empirical prior (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an explanation of why the hierarchical model performs better, with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: Speech sound categories are constantly revised as a function of the most recently presented stimuli.
source: Speech sound categories are constantly revised as a function of the most recently presented stimuli (Samuel and Kraljic, 2009; Kleinschmidt and Jaeger, 2015; Heald et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The proposed model provides a possible account for fast and transient changes in speech sound categories when confronted to a volatile sensory environment.
source: The proposed model provides a possible account for fast and transient changes in speech sound categories when confronted to a volatile sensory environment, involving the constant recalibration of internal models of speech.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's contribution.

claim: The reported effect in Lüttke et al. was distinct from other well-documented across-trial dependency effects, such as perceptual priming or selective adaptation.
source: Since the reported effect was distinct from other well-documented across-trial dependency effects, such as perceptual priming or selective adaptation (Heald et al., 2017; Gabay and Holt, 2018)
evidence: This is a claim about the uniqueness of the effect, supported by citations.

claim: The brain achieves perception by inverting a generative model.
source: Like previous approaches, ours builds on the idea that the brain achieves perception by inverting a generative model (e.g., Rao and Ballard, 1999; Knill and Pouget, 2004; Friston, 2005)
evidence: This is a theoretical framework supported by citations.

claim: The brain continuously monitors its performance to adapt internal models to changing stimulus landscapes.
source: and by continuously monitoring its performance to adapt it to changing stimulus landscapes.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about brain function.

claim: The brain can alter its internal models without external feedback by using the perceptual outcome as a teaching signal or ground truth to induce model recalibration.
source: One way the brain can alter its internal models without external feedback is by using the perceptual outcome as a teaching signal or ground truth (Luu and Stocker, 2018) to induce model recalibration, such that the outcome better explains the sensory features that produced it.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by a citation.

claim: The 'ideal adapter' framework uses update/learning rules giving equal weight to recent and past evidence.
source: In this framework, perceptual categories are subject to trial-by-trial changes well described by a Bayesian approach that implicitly assumes sound categories to be stable within an experimental session, and hence uses update/learning rules giving equal weight to recent and past evidence.
evidence: This is a description of the ideal adapter framework.

claim: The ideal adapter framework can describe the adaptation dynamics in sublexical speech categories in experiments with blocks of repeated stimuli.
source: While this makes sense in a stable environment where information remains equally relevant independent of its recency and the adaptation rule can describe the adaptation dynamics in sublexical speech categories in experiments with blocks of repeated stimuli (Bertelson et al., 2003; Vroomen et al., 2007)
evidence: This is a claim about the applicability of the ideal adapter framework, supported by citations.

claim: The ideal adapter framework failed to account for the specific transient effect in Lüttke et al.
source: it failed here to account for the specific transient effect in Lüttke et al. (2016b).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling comparison.

claim: Recalibration occurs at least at two levels, characterized by two different decaying timescales: a fast decaying/short-term process and a slow decaying/long-term process.
source: By comparing neurocomputational models with and without decay in their update rules, we show that recalibration occurs at least at two levels, characterized by two different decaying timescales: a fast decaying/short-term process (estimated to operate on the order of tens of seconds) that weighs recent versus immediate past sensory evidence, and a slow decaying/long-term process that keeps a longer trace of past sensory evidence to stabilize invariant representations.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by modeling results.

claim: The fast decaying process operates on the order of tens of seconds.
source: a fast decaying/short-term process (estimated to operate on the order of tens of seconds)
evidence: This is an estimate derived from the model parameters.

claim: A dual process is critical because speech sounds have both variable (e.g. speakers) and stable components (e.g. phonemic categories).
source: Such a dual process is critical because speech sounds have both variable (e.g. speakers) and stable components (e.g. phonemic categories).
evidence: This is a theoretical justification for the dual-timescale model.

claim: The fast changing variable in the model is driven by current sensory prediction errors, and the more slowly changing one is also driven by prediction errors but with a slower learning rate and hence acting as a longer-span buffer.
source: The fast changing variable is driven by current sensory prediction errors, and the more slowly changing one also driven by prediction errors but with a slower learning rate and hence acting as a longer-span buffer (Figure 5; Equation (8)).
evidence: This is a description of the model's mechanism with reference to Figure 5 and Equation 8.

claim: The parameter controlling the model expectations decays toward the longer-term parameter after a transient change driven by the current sensory prediction error.
source: As a result, the parameter controlling the model expectations decays toward the longer-term parameter after a transient change driven by the current sensory prediction error.
evidence: This is a description of the model's behavior.

claim: After a fused McGurk trial, the acoustic representation of /ada/ is shifted towards that of acoustic /aba/, which increases the chances of an acoustic /aba/ to be mis-categorized as 'ada'.
source: After a fused McGurk trial, the acoustic representation of /ada/ is shifted towards that of acoustic/aba/(Figure 3A), which increases the chances of an acoustic /aba/ to be mis-categorized as 'ada' (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a description of the model's behavior with reference to Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Since the recalibration decays over time, the mis-categorization is most prominent for the acoustic /aba/ immediately following the McGurk fusion.
source: Since the recalibration decays over time, the mis-categorization is most prominent for the acoustic /aba/ immediately following the McGurk fusion.
evidence: This is an inference about the model's behavior.

claim: Because the decay drifts towards a more slowly changing 'version' of the /ada/ category, the model can also accommodate a more persistent accumulated adaptation as experimentally observed.
source: On the other hand, because the decay drifts towards a more slowly changing 'version' of the /ada/ category, the model can also accommodate a more persistent accumulated adaptation as experimentally observed (Bertelson et al., 2003; Vroomen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a claim about the model's ability to explain experimental findings, supported by citations.

claim: The model is consistent with activity observed in auditory cortex.
source: The model, which encompasses both the perceptual decision and the recalibration processes, is also consistent with activity observed in auditory cortex (Lüttke et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is a claim about the model's consistency with neuroimaging data, supported by a citation.

claim: When the acoustic-only /aba/ was presented after a fused McGurk, fMRI activity in auditory cortex is more frequently classified as 'ada' by a learning algorithm.
source: When the acoustic-only /aba/ was presented after a fused McGurk, fMRI activity in auditory cortex is more frequently classified as 'ada' by a learning algorithm trained to distinguish correctly identified acoustic /aba/, /ada/ and /aga/.
evidence: This is a description of neuroimaging findings from the cited study.

claim: The intermediate level in the perceptual model corresponds to the representation of acoustic features in auditory cortex and visual features in extrastriate visual cortex.
source: The intermediate level in our perceptual model corresponds to the representation of acoustic features in auditory cortex and visual features in extrastriate visual cortex.
evidence: This is a theoretical mapping between the model and brain regions.

claim: In the model, the amplitude of the 2nd formant transition results from a combination of bottom-up sensory information and top-down predictions.
source: In our model the amplitude of the 2nd formant transition (the acoustic feature that is most important for the aba/ada contrast) results from a combination of bottom-up sensory information and top-down predictions (Equations 1, 2).
evidence: This is a description of the model's mechanism.

claim: Since there are more /aba/ sounds perceived as 'ada' after a fused McGurk, the top-down predictions during the perceptual process are dominated by the /ada/ category.
source: Since there are more /aba/ sounds perceived as 'ada' after a fused McGurk, the top-down predictions during the perceptual process are dominated by the /ada/ category
evidence: This is an inference about the model's internal state.

claim: The generative model predicts that activity in auditory cortex should be closer to /ada/ for acoustic /aba/ following fused McGurk trials, as shown by the fMRI data.
source: that is, our generative model predicts that activity in auditory cortex should be closer to /ada/ for acoustic /aba/ following fused McGurk trials, as shown by the fMRI data.
evidence: This is a claim that the model prediction matches neuroimaging data.

claim: During audiovisual speech integration, and in McGurk stimuli in particular, the brain tends to find the most parsimonious account of the input, merging the acoustic and visual sensory streams even at the expense of residual prediction errors.
source: In summary, during audiovisual speech integration, and in McGurk stimuli in particular, the brain tends to find the most parsimonious account of the input, merging the acoustic and visual sensory streams even at the expense of residual prediction errors at brain areas that encode unisensory stimulus features, represented in the model by the acoustic 2nd formant and lip amplitude modulation.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the model's behavior.

claim: Different participants may value differently the parsimony/accuracy trade-off.
source: Different participants may value differently this parsimony/accuracy trade-off.
evidence: This is a speculation about individual differences.

claim: Those who consistently fuse the two streams presumably recalibrate their category representations thereby reducing residual prediction errors at the feature level.
source: Those who consistently fuse the two streams presumably recalibrate their category representations (e.g. /ada/ after fused McGurk) thereby reducing residual prediction errors at the feature level.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the mechanism of recalibration.

claim: Recalibration does not happen primarily at the areas encoding the stimulus features, but at higher order areas that encode sub-lexical speech categories.
source: That is, we suggest that recalibration does not happen primarily at the areas encoding the stimulus features, but at higher order areas that encode sub-lexical speech categories, in a process that updates categories at least with two time scales.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about where recalibration occurs in the brain.

claim: Non-Bayesian abstract models of new speech category learning use Gaussian distributions with parameters that are updated with delta rules similar to Equation 7.
source: Some existing models involve processes that are similar to ours; for example, non-Bayesian abstract models of new speech category learning use Gaussian distributions with parameters that are updated with delta rules similar to that of Equation 7 (Vallabha et al., 2007a; McMurray et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous models, supported by citations.

claim: Connectionist models of speech category learning posit a first layer of units with a topographic representation of the sound feature space and a second layer representing individual speech categories.
source: On the other hand, connectionist models of speech category learning posit a first layer of units with a topographic representation of the sound feature space and a second layer representing individual speech categories.
evidence: This is a description of connectionist models from the literature.

claim: Mirman et al. modelled the recalibration of established prelexical categories that arises when an ambiguous sound is disambiguated by the lexical context as in the Ganong effect.
source: In this way, Mirman et al. (2006), modelled the recalibration of established prelexical categories that arises when an ambiguous sound is disambiguated by the lexical context as in the Ganong effect – a sound between /g/ and /k/ that tends to be classified as /g/ when preceding 'ift' or as /k/ when preceding 'iss' (Ganong, 1980).
evidence: This is a description of previous modeling work, supported by citations.

claim: The Ganong effect shares some similarities with the McGurk effect, although the latter is stronger as it changes the perception of a non-ambiguous sound.
source: This effect shares some similarities with the McGurk effect, although the latter is stronger as it changes the perception of a non-ambiguous sound.
evidence: This is a comparison between two perceptual effects.

claim: The benefit of having two timescales is illustrated by a connectionist model of the acquisition of non-native speech sound categories in the presence of well-established native ones.
source: The benefit of having two timescales is also illustrated by a connectionist model of the acquisition of non-native speech sound categories in the presence of well-established native ones (Vallabha and McClelland, 2007b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous modeling work.

claim: Interference between new and existing categories was avoided by positing a fast learning pathway applied to the novel categories, and a slower learning pathway to the native ones.
source: Interference between new and existing categories was avoided by positing a fast learning pathway applied to the novel categories, and a slower learning pathway to the native ones.
evidence: This is a description of a mechanism from previous modeling work.

claim: Connectionist models can reproduce short-term effects such as perceptual bias and habituation.
source: Finally, connectionist models can also reproduce short-term effects such as perceptual bias and habituation (Lancia and Winter, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous modeling work.

claim: A connectionist model could provide a physiologically plausible instantiation of the abstract Bayesian model as long as one incorporates two pathways with two different timescales or a single pathway that uses metastable synapses.
source: These examples suggest that a connectionist model could provide a physiologically plausible instantiation of our abstract Bayesian model as long as one incorporates two pathways with two different timescales or a single pathway that uses metastable synapses (Benna and Fusi, 2016).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by a citation.

claim: Parallel learning systems working at different temporal scales have previously been proposed in relation to speech.
source: Parallel learning systems working at different temporal scales have previously been proposed in relation to speech; one able to produce fast mappings and heavily relying on working memory, while the other relies on procedural learning structures that eventually results in effortless, implicit, associations (Myers and Mesite, 2014; Zeithamova et al., 2008; Maddox and Chandrasekaran, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: The brain implements at least two representations of natural categories; one more flexible than the other.
source: We argue that the brain implements at least two representations of natural categories; one more flexible than the other.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on the modeling results.

claim: The more flexible representation might be used to achieve the agent's current goal, while the more stable and less precise representation keeps general knowledge about sound categories.
source: The more flexible one might be used to achieve the agent's current goal, while the more stable and less precise representation keeps general knowledge about sound categories.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal about the functional roles of the two representations.

claim: The 'working representation' corresponds to an 'intermediate' representation that has lower uncertainty and therefore makes the sensory integration process more precise, leading to more confident perceptual decisions at the single trial level.
source: The 'working representation' corresponds to an 'intermediate' representation that has lower uncertainty and therefore makes the sensory integration process more precise, leading to more confident perceptual decisions at the single trial level.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the advantages of the working representation.

claim: This strategy allows the agent to use a precise 'working' category that can quickly change from trial to trial.
source: This strategy allows the agent to use a precise 'working' category that can quickly change from trial to trial.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the flexibility of the working representation.

claim: The agent needs to infer the distribution (mean and covariance) that defines the working representation, and combine sensory evidence with the prior (the corresponding long-term 'episodic' representation).
source: In this view, the agent needs to infer the distribution (mean and covariance) that defines the working representation, and combine sensory evidence with the prior, that is, with the corresponding long-term 'episodic' representation.
evidence: This is a theoretical description of the inference process.

claim: Bayesian inference assuming known volatilities for the two levels and under the mean-field approximation can be calculated analytically resulting in update equations that take the form written at the bottom of the diagram in Figure 6.
source: Bayesian inference assuming known volatilities for the two levels in Figure 6, and under the mean-field approximation, can be calculated analytically resulting in update equations that take the form written at the bottom of the diagram.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the mathematical derivation with reference to Figure 6.

claim: The coefficients in the update equations, which determine 'learning rates', are functions of the parameters of the model related to the different sources of uncertainty.
source: The coefficients, which determine what is referred to as 'learning rates' in the reinforcement learning literature, are functions of the parameters of the model related to the different sources of uncertainty: volatilities at both hierarchical levels, sensory noise and the width of the episodic representation.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation of the learning rate parameters.

claim: The proposed update equation assumes that agents have already estimated the volatilities at the two levels.
source: Our proposed update equation therefore assumes that agents have already estimated the volatilities at the two levels (as in Behrens et al., 2007; Nassar et al., 2010; Mathys et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an assumption of the model, supported by citations to related work.

claim: There are at least three scenarios that could support recalibration at different time scales.
source: There are at least three scenarios that could support recalibration at different time scales.
evidence: This introduces a discussion of possible neural implementations.

claim: A hierarchy of time scales might exist at the single synapse level.
source: First, a hierarchy of time scales might exist at the single synapse level.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about neural implementation.

claim: Hierarchically related variables with increasing time scales have been used in a modelling study to increase the capacity of memory systems and improve the stability of synaptic modifications.
source: Hierarchically related variables with increasing time scales (dynamics described by equations as in Figure 6B) have been used in a modelling study to increase the capacity of memory systems and improve the stability of synaptic modifications (Benna and Fusi, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous modeling work.

claim: A model of synapses with a cascade of metastable states with increasing stability was able to learn more flexibly under uncertainty.
source: and a model of synapses with a cascade of metastable states with increasing stability was able to learn more flexibly under uncertainty (Iigaya, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous modeling work.

claim: In the synaptic model, the intrinsic decay of synaptic modifications was faster for the more labile memory states.
source: In the latter model, the intrinsic decay of synaptic modifications was faster for the more labile memory states, i.e. those that are more sensitive to new evidence.
evidence: This is a description of a mechanism from previous modeling work.

claim: The deeper, more stable memory states in the synaptic model showed slower decay.
source: In contrast, the deeper, more stable memory states, showed slower decay, which overall nicely concurs with our proposal.
evidence: This is a comparison between previous work and the current proposal.

claim: It is possible that the representations are encoded at synapses with the transient recalibration corresponding to synaptic modification at the more labile states and the long-term component residing in the less labile states.
source: It is thereforepossible that the representations are encoded at synapses with the transient recalibration corresponding to synaptic modification at the more labile states and the long-term component residing in the less labile states.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about neural implementation.

claim: In perceptual classification tasks under volatile conditions, prefrontal cortex can flexibly combine alternative strategies.
source: In perceptual classification tasks under volatile conditions, prefrontal cortex can flexibly combine alternative strategies, such as optimal Bayesian-like learning in stable environments and a working memory model in volatile environments (Summerfield et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Prefrontal cortex could conceivably combine a 'working' short time scale representation of the speech categories with a long-term 'episodic' representation to guide speech classification.
source: In our setting, to guide the speech classification process, it could conceivably combine a 'working' short time scale representation of the speech categories with a long-term 'episodic' representation, which might reside in different brain networks.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about neural implementation.

claim: Several fronto-parietal regions have been implicated in controlling the effect of sensory and choice history on perceptual decisions.
source: Several fronto-parietal regions have indeed been implicated in controlling the effect of sensory and choice history on perceptual decisions: 'Sensory evidence, choice and outcome' could be decoded from ventrolateral prefrontal cortex and predicted choice biases (Tsunada et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Neuronal responses in fronto-parietal circuits could provide a basis for flexible timescales.
source: Neuronal responses in fronto-parietal circuits could provide a basis for flexible timescales (Scott et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Dissociated effects of working memory and past sensory history have been found to involve the prefrontal cortex and posterior parietal cortices respectively.
source: as dissociated effects of working memory and past sensory history have been found to involve the prefrontal cortex and posterior parietal cortices respectively (Akrami et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The observed sensitivity to sensory choice history and sensory evidence is consistent with the model, which uses internal category representations to interpret sensory evidence, with category representations being recalibrated based on choice.
source: The observed sensitivity to sensory choice history and sensory evidence is consistent with our model, which uses internal category representations to interpret sensory evidence, with category representations being recalibrated based on choice (i.e., the perceived category).
evidence: This is a claim about consistency between the model and neurophysiological findings.

claim: The hierarchical nature of perception and action might be paralleled in the brain by hierarchical processing in prefrontal cortex and sensory areas.
source: Finally, the hierarchical nature of perception and action (Kiebel et al., 2008; Friston, 2008) might be paralleled in the brain, by hierarchical processing in prefrontal cortex (Badre, 2008; Koechlin and Jubault, 2006; Summerfield et al., 2006) and sensory areas (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Chevillet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by multiple citations.

claim: It is conceivable that the relation between the two timescales is hierarchical with higher-level representations becoming increasingly abstract and time insensitive.
source: It is hence conceivable that the relation between the two timescales is hierarchical with higher-level representations becoming increasingly abstract and time insensitive.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about neural organization.

claim: The brain might use representations at a speaker level that are drawn from more general representations of speech categories at the population level.
source: This could happen, for example, if the brain used representations at a speaker level that are drawn from more general representations of speech categories at the population level.
evidence: This is a speculative example of hierarchical organization.

claim: Recalibration might work at every level of the temporal hierarchy, with higher levels integrating update information within increasingly longer time windows.
source: Recalibration might work at every level of the temporal hierarchy, with higher levels integrating update information within increasingly longer time windows (longer timescales), making them less and less sensitive to new observations.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about how recalibration might work hierarchically.

claim: The 'ideal adapter' account focused on cumulative recalibration.
source: While the 'ideal adapter' account focused on cumulative recalibration (Kleinschmidt and Jaeger, 2015)
evidence: This is a characterization of previous work, supported by a citation.

source: our results suggest that shorter-lived effects are also behaviorally relevant.

source: The ideal adapter could be formalized as a simple incremental optimal Bayesian inference in a non-volatile environment (Figure 6, left panel)
evidence: This is a theoretical characterization with reference to Figure 6.

claim: The update rule in the current model could be cast in a normative framework that explicitly accounts for environmental volatility.
source: whereas our update rule could be cast in a normative framework that explicitly accounts for environmental volatility.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the model's framework.

claim: A hierarchical model with constant volatility at two levels could lead to hierarchical update equations that can be approximated by constant learning rates.
source: A hierarchical model with constant volatility at two levels (Figure 6, right panel) could lead to hierarchical update equations (Wilson et al., 2013) that can be approximated by constant learning rates (with higher learning rates - faster 'forgetting'- being related to stronger volatility).

claim: The hierarchical model assumes that the higher level (μ) has lower volatility than the intermediate level (θ), hence combining volatility with hierarchy.
source: The right panel of Figure 6 assumes that the higher level (μ) has lower volatility than the intermediate level (θ), hence combining volatility with hierarchy.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure with reference to Figure 6.

claim: This combination departs from models used to explain decision making in changing environments, which are not hierarchical, and focus on the nontrivial task of inferring the environment volatility.
source: This combination departs from models used to explain decision making in changing environments (Behrens et al., 2007; Summerfield et al., 2011; Mathys et al., 2014), which are not hierarchical, and focus on the nontrivial task of inferring the environment volatility.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous models, supported by citations.

claim: Studies show that human participants adapt their learning rates to the changing volatility.
source: These studies show that human participants adapt their learning rates to the changing volatility, which could be modelled without keeping representations across several time scales.
evidence: This is a description of findings from previous studies.

claim: In previous decision-making tasks, participants need to keep track of short-lived changes in arbitrary cue-reward associations or in arbitrarily defined sensory categories.
source: In these tasks, participants need to keep track of short-lived changes in arbitrary cue-reward associations or in arbitrarily defined sensory categories (Summerfield et al., 2011)
evidence: This is a description of previous experimental paradigms, supported by a citation.

claim: The current model deals with overlearned and behaviourally relevant categories, which also requires maintaining long-term estimates as empirical priors.
source: whereas we model overlearned and behaviourally relevant categories, which also requires to maintain long-term estimates as empirical priors.
evidence: This is a distinction between the current model and previous models.

claim: The modelling results are relevant to continuous speech processing, in particular to account for auditory processing anomalies in dyslexia.
source: Our modelling results are relevant to continuous speech processing, in particular to account for auditory processing anomalies in dyslexia.
evidence: This is a claim about the broader relevance of the findings.

claim: Evidence from a two-tone frequency discrimination task suggests that participants' choices are driven not only by the tones presented at a given trial, but also by the recent history of tone frequencies in the experiment.
source: Evidence from a two-tone frequency discrimination task suggests that participants' choices are driven not only by the tones presented at a given trial, but also by the recent history of tone frequencies in the experiment, with recent tones having more weight than earlier ones (Jaffe-Dax et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: When compared with controls, subjects with dyslexia show a decreased reliance on temporally distant tones, suggesting a shorter time constant.
source: It turns out that, when compared with controls, subjects with dyslexia show a decreased reliance on temporally distant tones, suggesting a shorter time constant (Jaffe-Dax et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: In dyslexia, the long-term component (μ) might have either a shorter time span, or be coupled to the lower representation with a lower weight.
source: Translating this result to the current model, we could hypothesize that in dyslexia the long-term component (μ in Figure 6B) has either a shorter time span, or is coupled to the lower representation with a lower weight.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on translating experimental findings to the model.

claim: In both cases (shorter time span or lower coupling weight), we would expect a deficit in building long-term stable speech category representations since they would be overly driven by the current context.
source: In both cases, we would expect a deficit in building long-term stable speech category representations since they would be overly driven by the current context.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model.

claim: ASD individuals are optimally biased by long-term tones, but do not show the bias by short-term tones of neurotypical participants.
source: ASD individuals on the other hand, are optimally biased by long-term tones, but do not show the bias by short-term tones of neurotypical participants (Lieder et al., 2019)

source: We present a revised 'ideal adapter' model for speech sound recalibration that has both transient and cumulative components organized hierarchically.

source: This new model provides evidence for a hierarchy of processes in the recalibration of speech categories

claim: After experiencing the McGurk effect, it is not the acoustic features related to the sensory input that are modified, but higher-level syllabic representations.
source: and highlights that after experiencing the McGurk effect, it is not the acoustic features related to the sensory input that are modified, but higher-level syllabic representations.

source: The model implies that the activity changes in sensory cortices are not locally generated but reflect the interaction of bottom-up peripheral sensory inputs and top-down expectations from regions where categorical perception takes place.

claim: Considering natural speech processing as the inversion of a continuously monitored and recalibrated internal model can unveil the potential operations and strategies that listeners use when confronted with acoustic volatility.
source: Considering natural speech processing as the inversion of a continuously monitored and recalibrated internal model can unveil the potential operations and strategies that listeners use when they are confronted with the acoustic volatility associated with speech categories, which by their nature have both rapidly changing (e.g. speaker specific) and slowly changing (e.g. speaker general) components.

claim: The model can be implemented by a hierarchy of empirical priors that are subject to changes at different time scales.
source: Such a model can be implemented by a hierarchy of empirical priors that are subject to changes at different time scales.

claim: Although developed in the context of speech processing, the proposal may also apply to other cognitive domains requiring perhaps more nested timescales, such as action planning.
source: Although developed in the context of speech processing, our proposal may also apply to other cognitive domains requiring perhaps more nested timescales, such as action planning (Badre, 2008; Koechlin and Summerfield, 2007; Koechlin et al., 2003).
